::: {.why}
Removing one signal from another produces a third thing whose economic meaning you have to be able to state, and if you cannot state it you have made an estimation decision rather than a modelling one.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Orthogonalise one signal against another and say what the residual is a forecast of.
- Say why the order of orthogonalisation matters and what a symmetric alternative would be.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Explore the asymmetry: orthogonalise A against B, then B against A, and evaluate both residuals. The results differ and the difference is not a bug; sequential orthogonalisation assigns shared explanatory power to whichever came first. Report both and note which ordering you would defend.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Implement the symmetric alternative: whitening the signal set so all components are orthogonal without privileging an order, then evaluate the resulting components. Note that the components are combinations rather than signals, so their economic interpretation is weaker, which is the trade you are making.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the decision for the book: orthogonalise where the economics dictate an ordering, otherwise handle correlation in the weighting rather than in the signals.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Both orthogonalisation orderings evaluated plus a whitened component set, with the written policy for the book.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
You orthogonalise value against quality. What is the residual a forecast of, and what would the other ordering have given you?
:::
